title: Collect employee names into a `Set<String>` (removing duplicates).
shortTitle: Collect employee names into a Set<String> (removing duplicates)

s1_definition.profdef: `map(Employee::getName).collect(Collectors.toSet())` gathers names into a `Set`, which inherently removes duplicates because a set holds each distinct value once.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya lists the unique names of employees — if two people have the same name, it appears only once.
s1_definition.oneliner: `map(name).collect(toSet())` collects distinct names, dropping duplicates automatically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `map(Employee::getName).collect(Collectors.toSet())` gathers names into a `Set`, which inherently removes duplicates because a set holds each distinct value once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya lists the unique names of employees — if two people have the same name, it appears only once.

**One line to remember:** `map(name).collect(toSet())` collects distinct names, dropping duplicates automatically.

sections.s2_technical:
`staff.stream().map(Employee::getName).collect(Collectors.toSet())` maps each employee to a name and collects into a `Set<String>`. Because a set stores each element once by equals and hashCode, duplicate names are automatically dropped — no explicit distinct is needed.

`toSet` returns a HashSet by default, so iteration order is unspecified. If I need sorted or insertion order I use `toCollection(TreeSet::new)` or `toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new)`. The deduplication relies on String's correct equals and hashCode, which it has.

The senior nuance is that `toSet` gives no ordering guarantee and no control over the concrete type, so when ordering or a specific set type matters I use `toCollection` with a supplier. `toSet` deduplicating is equivalent to `distinct().collect(toList())` but expresses the set intent directly. For custom objects, deduplication depends entirely on their equals and hashCode being correct.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A mailing list at the National Bank of India needs the set of distinct employee names, with duplicates removed.

This is exactly what collecting to a set does — it keeps each name once.

The code defines a `MailingListService.distinctNames method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh, Priya, and a second Rajesh.

Step 1: map extracts the three names.

Step 2: toSet collects them into a HashSet.

Step 3: The second Rajesh is a duplicate by equals and hashCode, so it is not added again.

Step 4: The set contains two distinct names.

```
INFO: Distinct names: [Rajesh, Priya] (size=2)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To collect distinct employee names I map each employee to its name and collect with Collectors toSet, which gathers them into a set. Because a set stores each element only once by equals and hashCode, duplicate names are removed automatically — I do not need an explicit distinct step. At the National Bank of India this backs a mailing list that needs each name once.

toSet returns a HashSet by default, so there is no ordering guarantee and no control over the concrete type. When ordering matters I use toCollection with a TreeSet supplier for sorted order or a LinkedHashSet supplier for insertion order instead. The deduplication relies on correct equals and hashCode, which String provides.

The senior point I stress is that for custom objects, deduplication is only as good as their equals and hashCode — if those are not implemented correctly, the set will not dedupe as expected. toSet expresses the set intent directly and is equivalent to calling distinct and collecting to a list, but it communicates that I want uniqueness as the primary goal. When I need a specific set type or ordering, toCollection with a supplier is the tool.
